title: How to collaborate on a shared presentation in Keynote on Mac: steps for Keynote 15.4
metaTitle: Collaborate on a Shared Keynote Presentation on Mac
description: How to collaborate on a shared presentation in Keynote on Mac: share a link, set who can edit, and add people later. Steps for Keynote 15.4.
targetKeyword: how to collaborate on a shared presentation in keynote on mac
intro: To collaborate on a shared presentation in Keynote on Mac, store the file in iCloud Drive, click Share in the toolbar, and choose Share a Link. Set Who can access and Permissions, then send the link by Mail, Messages, Notes or Copy Link, and your collaborators can start editing with you.
tldr: Requirements: macOS 26 or later, Keynote 15.4 or later, an Apple Account, and iCloud Drive turned on for Keynote.
Share by clicking Share, choosing Share a Link, opening the disclosure arrow, then setting Who can access and Permissions.
Pick Only invited people or Anyone with the link, and Can make changes or View only.
Add people later with File > Manage Shared Presentation, then Share With More People.
To leave, open Manage Shared Presentation, hover over your name, click More, and choose Remove Me.

blocks.text: Keynote sharing works through iCloud Drive, not through files you email back and forth. The presentation lives in one place, and everyone with access sees the same slides. That is why setup has three parts: an Apple Account, iCloud Drive turned on for Keynote, and the file stored in iCloud Drive. Get those right first, and the share itself takes only a few clicks.
What you need before you share

Apple's guide to collaboration in Keynote on Mac lists three requirements. You need to be signed in to an Apple Account. Keynote needs iCloud Drive turned on for it. And the presentation has to live in iCloud Drive. If the file sits somewhere else, Keynote prompts you to move it. Accept the prompt and you are ready to share.

items: Signed in to an Apple Account on your Mac
iCloud Drive turned on for Keynote in System Settings
The presentation stored in iCloud Drive
macOS 26 or later on every Mac that edits
Keynote 15.4 or later on Mac, iPhone and iPad
A file under 2 GB, or under 4 GB with Creator Studio

blocks.text: Version numbers matter more than most people expect. Keynote 15.4 for Mac requires macOS 26 or later. Collaborators on iPhone and iPad need iOS 26 or later and Keynote 15.4 or later. A person on an older version can still open the file to view it, but they cannot edit. Ask everyone to check before you send the link, not after the first edit fails. Keynote 15.4 also adds a Request access to collaborate on a shared presentation option for all users, according to Apple's What's new page.
Share a presentation with a link, step by step

The steps below follow the Share a Link route. Apple describes this route for collaboration in Keynote 15.4, and it covers most cases. You open the Share button, pick a link, decide who can get in, and decide what those people can do. Then you send the link by Mail, Messages, Notes, or the clipboard.

Menu labels come from Apple's guide. Keynote can look a little different from one macOS build to the next, so if a label is missing, look for the same words in the Share pop-up. Apple's pages also do not agree on every permission name, which the next section covers.
Choose who can access and what they can do

Two settings control the link. Who can access has two choices, Only invited people and Anyone with the link. Permissions also has two choices, Can make changes and View only. Mix them to fit the job. A team that edits one deck every day usually wants invited people who can make changes. A deck for a wider audience, shared for review, may fit Anyone with the link set to View only.

blocks.caption: Access and permission options in the Share a Link pop-up
rows: Only people you invite can open the presentation
Anyone who receives the link can open it
Recipients can view but cannot reply to or delete comments in the activity list

blocks.text: View only has a limit you should know. Viewers cannot reply to or delete comments in the activity list. No join notifications appear for them either. If you need feedback in the activity list, give people Can make changes. Apple's web page for Keynote for iCloud uses the words edit and view instead, so the labels can differ slightly depending on where you look.
Add people after you share
Adding people later is simple, but only the owner or someone with permission from the owner can do it. Apple describes three routes to the same panel. Pick whichever sits closest to your hand.

items: Choose File > Manage Shared Presentation in the menu bar
Click the Collaboration button in the toolbar, then choose Manage Shared Presentation
Control-click the file in iCloud Drive, then choose Manage Shared Presentation

blocks.text: Click Share With More People to send new invitations. Apple describes this route for presentations set to Only invited people. If you see a different button, check the access setting first. The Who can access pop-up decides which invitation path applies.
What happens while people edit

Edits by collaborators appear in real time. You can keep working when your connection drops. The Collaboration button then shows a cloud with a diagonal line. When you reconnect, your edits upload. To check where things stand, choose View > Show Sync Status.

One edge case catches people. If someone else deleted an object while you were offline, your edits to that object are not incorporated. Check the slide after you reconnect, especially if you worked on a chart or image that a colleague may have removed.

Conflicts happen when a presentation is edited on several devices before the changes have time to sync. Keynote then opens a dialog and asks you to choose which version to keep. The most recent version you keep becomes the shared version. Apple says you can keep any or all versions, but only for presentations that are not shared with others. For a shared file, read the dialog carefully before you click.
Limits and locked features

Up to 100 people can view and edit a shared presentation at the same time. That is a lot of people for one deck, so the limit rarely matters for a class or a team meeting. File size matters more. A document over 2 GB must be reduced before you invite others. Apple Creator Studio subscribers get a 4 GB limit.

Some features stay locked while the file is shared. Changing the slide size or the theme is blocked. So are recording slideshows and editing soundtracks. Apple's workaround is to stop sharing, make the change, and share again. That removes the file from iCloud Drive for every participant, so warn your team before you do it.

blocks.title: Stopping a share affects everyone
blocks.text: Stopping sharing to change the theme or slide size removes the file from iCloud Drive for all participants. Finish layout and theme work before you send the link.
Keynote for iCloud in a web browser

Not everyone will open the Mac app. Keynote for iCloud runs in a browser. Apple says it needs a supported browser on a Mac with macOS 14.0 or later, or on a Windows device. Safari 13.1 or later, Chrome, or Edge can open it at iCloud.com. On the web, the owner's Add People button replaces the Share pop-up, if the owner allowed it.

Two things differ on the web. Apple's guide places the detailed Show All Activity change list in the Mac, iPhone and iPad apps, so it does not appear to be on the web. Search also changes. Command-F on a Mac, or Control-F on Windows, searches for a presentation by name in the document manager. Apple lists no other keyboard shortcut for sharing.
Leave a shared presentation

Leaving is reversible, which makes it a safe move when a project ends. Click the Collaboration button, choose Manage Shared Presentation, hover over your name, click More, choose Remove Me, and click Done. The presentation leaves your iCloud Drive. Open the original link again and it comes back.
Mistakes people make with shared decks
Most problems come from four habits. Each one has a simple fix, and each one shows up in the same few places in the Share pop-up and the Collaboration panel.

items: Sending the link before checking versions. Anyone on an older macOS or Keynote build can only view.
Choosing Anyone with the link for a deck that should stay internal. Switch to Only invited people first.
Editing offline on two devices, then reconnecting. Expect a conflict dialog and check each slide afterward.
Changing the theme or slide size mid-project. Stopping sharing removes the file for everyone.

blocks.text: Give the team a shared rule before you start. Agree who makes structural changes and who only comments. Then set Permissions to match that plan. Teams that skip this step usually fix permissions after someone has already changed the theme.

Once the deck is shared, the next work is usually content. [Reorder slides in Keynote](/how-to/reorder-slides-in-keynote) covers the drag, outline and Light Table options. [Add presenter notes](/how-to/add-presenter-notes-in-keynote) shows how to keep your own notes out of the room. Teachers running shared class decks can start with [Keynote for teachers on Mac](/for/teachers/keynote).

faq.question: Do I need Keynote 15.4 to collaborate in Keynote on Mac?
faq.answer: Yes, for editing. Apple says collaborators need Keynote 15.4 or later on Mac, and the same version on iPhone and iPad. Check Keynote > About Keynote on each Mac before you send the link. A device below the requirements can still view the file.

faq.question: Can people with Android phones edit a shared Keynote presentation?
faq.answer: No. Apple says Android users can view a shared presentation but cannot edit it. A person with a Windows device can use Keynote for iCloud in a supported browser, which is the web route Apple describes.

faq.question: How many people can edit a shared Keynote presentation at once?
faq.answer: Up to 100 people can view and edit a shared presentation at the same time, according to Apple's collaboration guide. Stay well under that number for smooth editing on busy decks.

faq.question: Why do I have to be the owner to add people?
faq.answer: Apple says you need to be the owner, or have permission from the owner, to invite more people to an Only invited people presentation. If you are not the owner, ask the owner to add the person in Manage Shared Presentation.

faq.question: Can I change the theme while a presentation is shared?
faq.answer: Not while it stays shared. Apple lists slide size and theme changes as blocked during collaboration. You must stop sharing, make the change, and share again, which removes the file from iCloud Drive for all participants.

faq.question: What file size can I share in Keynote?
faq.answer: Files over 2 GB must be reduced before you invite others. Apple Creator Studio subscribers have a 4 GB limit. Remove unused images and large video files before you share, if the deck is close to the limit.

faq.question: Do I lose my copy of the presentation when I remove myself?
faq.answer: Removing yourself takes the presentation out of your iCloud Drive. Reopen the original link and the file returns to your iCloud Drive. Apple describes this as reversible.

steps.name: Check macOS and Keynote versions
steps.text: Every person who edits needs macOS 26 or later and Keynote 15.4 or later on Mac. Open Apple menu > About This Mac to check macOS. Then open Keynote > About Keynote to check the app version.
steps.tip: A device on an older version can view the presentation, but it cannot edit.

steps.name: Sign in to your Apple Account
steps.text: Keynote needs an Apple Account for collaboration. Open System Settings and look at your name at the top of the sidebar. If you see Sign In instead, sign in before you go further.

steps.name: Turn on iCloud Drive for Keynote
steps.text: Click your name, then choose iCloud. Under Saved to iCloud, click See All, turn on Keynote, and click Done.
steps.tip: If Keynote is already turned on in this list, skip this step.

steps.name: Move the presentation to iCloud Drive
steps.text: Open the presentation. If it is not in iCloud Drive, Keynote prompts you to move it. Accept the prompt, then check that the file appears in iCloud Drive.

steps.name: Click Share in the toolbar
steps.text: Click the Share button in the Keynote toolbar. A pop-up menu opens with the sharing options.

steps.name: Choose Share a Link
steps.text: In the pop-up menu, choose Share a Link.

steps.name: Open the disclosure arrow and set access
steps.text: Click the disclosure arrow to show more settings. Open the Who can access pop-up and choose Only invited people or Anyone with the link.
steps.tip: Use Only invited people when the deck contains anything you would not post publicly.

steps.name: Set Permissions
steps.text: Open the Permissions pop-up. Choose Can make changes for people who should edit, or View only for people who should only look.
steps.tip: View only viewers cannot reply to or delete comments in the activity list.

steps.name: Send the link
steps.text: Send the link by Mail or Messages, or through Notes with Share Link. You can also click Copy Link and paste it wherever you need it. A checkmark then appears on the Collaboration button.
steps.tip: Send the link only to people who should have it, especially with Anyone with the link selected.

steps.name: Add people later
steps.text: Choose File > Manage Shared Presentation, or click the Collaboration button and choose Manage Shared Presentation. Then click Share With More People and send the invitations.
steps.tip: You must be the owner or have permission from the owner.

steps.name: Leave a shared presentation
steps.text: Click the Collaboration button and choose Manage Shared Presentation. Hover over your name, click More, choose Remove Me, and click Done.
steps.tip: Removing yourself takes the file out of your iCloud Drive. Reopen the original link to bring it back.

troubleshooting.problem: Keynote will not let me share the file
troubleshooting.fix: Check that you are signed in to an Apple Account, that iCloud Drive is turned on for Keynote, and that the file sits in iCloud Drive. If it is somewhere else, Keynote prompts you to move it.

troubleshooting.problem: A cloud with a diagonal line appears on the Collaboration button
troubleshooting.fix: You are offline. Your edits stay on your device and upload when you reconnect. Choose View > Show Sync Status to see what is still waiting.

troubleshooting.problem: A conflict dialog appears after two devices edit the same deck
troubleshooting.fix: Choose which version to keep. The most recent kept version becomes the shared version. Check the slides afterward, because Apple says keeping several versions applies only to presentations that are not shared.

troubleshooting.problem: A collaborator can open the file but cannot edit it
troubleshooting.fix: Their device is below the requirements. They need macOS 26 or later and Keynote 15.4 or later on Mac, or iOS 26 or later and Keynote 15.4 or later on iPhone or iPad. Android users can only view.

troubleshooting.problem: I need to change the theme or slide size
troubleshooting.fix: Those changes are blocked while the file is shared. Stop sharing, make the change, and share again. Stopping removes the file from iCloud Drive for all participants, so tell the team first.

troubleshooting.problem: An object I edited offline has disappeared
troubleshooting.fix: Apple says edits to objects that others deleted while you were offline are not incorporated. Recreate the object if you still need it, then check the slide for anything else that changed.
